statements.text: AI, as I read in Dr. Wang's testimony—Mr. Wang's testimony—brings potential benefit, potential risk. We have seen the abuse of AI in China for public surveillance and crackdowns.
statements.context: House hearing on AI technology, human discovery, and American global competitiveness.

statements.text: And Dr. Schmidt, basically, same question. If we don't have good transmission and the ability to move energy across the country, how does that impact our ability to remain dominant and win the AI race?
statements.context: Rep. Schrier poses a question to Dr. Eric Schmidt during a hearing on AI technology, human discovery, and American global competitiveness.

statements.text: we should all be very concerned about the potential dangers posed. And, yes, absolutely Big Tech needs certainty about regulation, but that should not be in the form of a guarantee of no regulation for 10 years. [...] Congress just passed the TAKE IT DOWN Act. [...] But the AI moratorium that Republicans sneaked into their tax bill would in yet another way hurt Americans by preventing any State from providing even greater protections against AI child pornography or other AI products that hurt our kids.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Kim Schrier (D-WA) at a congressional hearing on AI regulation and U.S. leadership.

statements.text: Unfortunately, in a giant gift to Big Tech, committee Republicans supported a provision in their terrible tax bill last week that imposes a 10-year ban on any State's ability to enforce their own laws protecting consumers from the harms caused by AI.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Kim Schrier at a House Energy and Commerce Committee hearing on AI regulation and federal-state preemption.

statements.text: when you have AI giving one answer and a physician giving another answer and something goes wrong, I think we need to think hard about where the liability is, is it on the AI company or is it on the physician, and the toll that that takes on physicians also to be a checkpoint and also to just be a reviewer of loads of data.
statements.context: Closing remarks by Rep. Schrier at a congressional hearing on AI in American health care.

statements.text: And then I try to — you know, companies try to reassure me by telling me don't worry. Every hour, we are going to post that I am not a real person. I am a chatbot. Don't worry. If any of these cue words come up, we are going to say call 988.
statements.context: House Energy & Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI chatbot risks and benefits, featuring expert witnesses.

statements.text: I am going to first talk about AI, because the new AI frontier has brought new vulnerabilities — and benefits — to the grid, and also to our broader society, both because of reliance on AI by virtually every industry out there and because AI can be used to foster resiliency in our grid. But it could also be used to sabotage our grid by bad actors.
statements.context: House Energy and Commerce subcommittee hearing on securing America's energy infrastructure against cyber and physical threats.

statements.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. It feels like we are going to just have to keep pace with this. I am wondering, do you think that we should just have a fresh evaluation of NERC's Critical Infrastructure Protection standards in light of AI and the new threats and the quick evolution of those threats?
statements.context: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee hearing on securing the U.S. energy infrastructure against cyber and physical threats to the grid.

statements.text: And so, I am so supportive of Representative McClellan's bill to increase data transparency in Medicare Advantage and Representative Landsman's bill to stop the use of AI and prior authorization and the expansion of that true traditional Medicare.
statements.context: Rep. Schrier speaks during a House Energy & Commerce Health Subcommittee hearing on Medicare access and prior authorization abuses.

statements.text: AI brings both tremendous opportunity and risk. [...] AI impacts are a really big concern for my constituents in Washington State. The people I represent are worried about what the emergence of AI means for their jobs, for their privacy, and, specific to this hearing, for their utility bills and keeping the lights on.
statements.context: Opening statement by Rep. Kim Schrier (D-WA) at a House Energy & Commerce subcommittee hearing on AI's impact on power-grid demand and ratepayers.
